article_text:
A new role has been announced at London’s National Portrait Gallery – the CHANEL Curator of Photography

London’s National Portrait Gallery and CHANEL Culture Fund have teamed up to create a new post, the CHANEL Curator of Photography. The role is the first medium-specific role CHANEL has supported at the NPG, and builds on a partnership with the gallery dating back to 2020. The first CHANEL Curator of Photography will be announced later this Autumn.

Between 2020-25, CHANEL Culture Fund supported the CHANEL Curator for the Collection at NPG, for example, held by Dr. Flavia Frigeri. Now Chief Curator at the NPG, Frigeri was responsible for the Reframing Narratives: Women in Portraiture project, which readdressed the gender imbalance in the NPG’s collection through acquisitions, research and site-specific commissions. This initiative included the Madame Yevonde project, which funded the conservation, research, cataloguing, and digitisation of Yevonde’s 2000 tri-colour separation negatives, acquired by NPG in 2021. The exhibition Yevonde: Life and Colour, which ran from 22 June – 15 October 2023 and featured over 150 words by the pioneering image-maker, was also directly supported by CHANEL Culture Fund.

“The National Portrait Gallery’s photographs collection spans more than 250,000 images from the 1840s to today,” comments Frigeri of the new CHANEL Curator of Photography role. “The new Chanel post will raise the collection’s profile by supporting research and the development of a future strategy.”

CHANEL Culture Fund also recently invited NPG to curate an exhibition at CHANEL Nexus Hall in Ginza, Tokyo, on show until 29 November. Icons and Image Makers: Photographs from the National Portrait Gallery includes 59 photographs of British icons drawn from the NPG’s collection, including Jack Davison’s 2016 portrait of Ruth Negga, and Tami Aftab’s 2021 photograph of Olivia Dean, as well as work by Irving Penn, Juergen Teller, and many others. The exhibition is CHANEL’s Cultural Fund’s first exhibition with one of its partner institutions to be held in Japan.

“ The National Portrait Gallery’s photographs collection spans more than 250,000 images from the 1840s to today. The new Chanel post will raise the collection’s profile by supporting research and the development of a future strategy.” Dr Flavia Frigeri, chief curator, NPG

CHANEL Cultural Fund is partnered with many art institutions around the world, including Centre Pompidou, Paris; Power Station of Art, Shanghai; Leeum Museum of Art, Seoul; and Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago. It was also the main sponsor of the French Pavilion at the 60th Venice Biennale. The Fund also supports photography-specific initiatives, including the Kyotographie International Photography Festival, and supported British artist Linder’s first exhibitions in Japan at both Kyotographie and at CHANEL Nexus Hall. In early 2026 CHANEL Nexus Hall commissioned US photographer Roe Ethridge to create a series of collages exploring Gabrielle Chanel’s possessions, which was also shown at both CHANEL Nexus Hall and Kyotographie – as was an earlier solo show by Indian image-maker Pushpamala N.

The fund supports the Jimei x Arles International Photography Festival, co-founding the Curatorial Award for Photography and Moving Image with festival-organiser Three Shadows Photography Art Centre in 2021. Helping nurture the next generation of Chinese curators and researchers through open calls, master classes, project funding, and mentorship, this award invites selected artist/curator duos to submit proposals, then helps develop and support these proposals. Selected proposals are presented at the festival in a group show, with one winning proposal selected for further realisation and touring.

The group show this year is titled Afterglow, and goes on show in the Jimei x Arles festival from 17 November – 03 January. Curated by Rachel Wuang, it brings together work by six artists exploring stereotypes of Northeast China; Gu Tao, Hu Weiyi, Li Yong, Liu Yujia, Tong Yutian, and Yi Changhong. The 2026 residency for the next edition will take place alongside the Jimei x Arles opening week; themed ‘The Generative Eye’, it includes rising curator He Yining as the mentor, alongside senior curators Carol Yinghua Lu and Liu Ding.

CHANEL Cultural Fund also creates an annual publication, Arts & Culture, which launched its second issue in October. The 300-page issue featured work by Linder and NPG director Victoria Siddall, as well as new work by Cindy Sherman. The work featured is from Sherman’s Fabric Matrons series, which includes fabric and jewellery the artist was invited to incorporate from Chanel’s archive; Sherman’s collaboration with Chanel dates back to her Ominous Landscapes series from 2010-2012, in which she also created characters wearing garments and accessories from Chanel’s archive. Works from the Fabric Matrons series are on show at Hauser & Wirth, London until 23 December.

Arts & Culture is distributed free of charge at selected art institutions and bookshops, including Paris’ Librarie 7L, which is owned by Chanel. The magazine does not carry ads, apart from publicity for the partner bookshops, which are given to the stores free of charge. Arts & Culture is produced under the direction of Yana Peel, President of Arts, Culture & Heritage at Chanel.

“At the heart of the work of the CHANEL Culture Fund is cultivating care for ideas, for artists, and for the irreplaceable act of making something new,” says Peel. “Our ARTS & CULTURE magazine is where that practice leaves its trace. There could be no one better to grace the cover of Vol.2 than Cindy Sherman, who for five decades has examined the construction of identity and the power over personae that women hold. In her photographs, she renders the modern woman – and her freedom of becoming – with empowerment and care.”

article_text:
As the art market in the Middle East heats up with the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi taking place next month, the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening in December, and Art Basel Qatar expected to return for its second edition in 2027, Sotheby’s is deepening its activity in the region with the launch of the house’s first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi on December 10, a day before the Guggenheim opening.

Part of Sotheby’s Collectors’ Week, which debuted last year, the upcoming second edition returns with categories including cars, jewelry, watches, high-performance bicycles and handbags to hit the hammer on December 9. The dedicated fine art sale has been titled “Breaking Ground,” a nod to how the city has been “forged from the ground up,” per a release, and will be hosted at the new Saadiyat Grove Experience Center on Saadiyat Island, the city’s cultural hub.

Sotheby’s is expected to add more lots to the sale before December, but released a suite of 21 that it has confirmed so far. As of now, the sale’s low estimate is $6.54 million and the high estimate is $9.08 million.

The top two lots are Andy Warhol’s Ads (1985) with an estimate of $2 million to $3 million and Claude Monet’s Prunes et Abricots (1882–85) with an estimate of $2 million to $2.6 million. The collection heavily features Emirati contemporary artists like Mohamed Ahmed Ibrahim and Hassan Sharif, as well as artworks made by women such as Huguette Caland, Jadé Fadojutimi, Inji Efflatoun, Fahrelnissa Zeid, Najat Makki, Mona Saudi, Gazbia Sirry, Zarina, and Etel Adnan.

Katia Nounou Boueiz, head of Sotheby’s UAE and chairman of the Middle East, told ARTnews that although the auction house has been active in the region for quite some time, clients from the region have increasingly been a strong force at the international auctions. “The past five years have seen a significant increase in bidding—nearly 70 percent—from the Middle East, while the total value spent by clients has grown by almost 100 percent,” she said. Sotheby’s had its first international cross-category art auction in Dubai, titled “Boundless,” back in 2017.

Abu Dhabi of late is becoming a hot spot, and December has a host of events that will likely attract collectors, celebrities, royal families, and politicians: the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix (December 3–6), the Abu Dhabi Finance Week conference (December 7–10), and the Culture Summit Abu Dhabi (December 8–10). Boueiz said Sotheby’s first international fine art auction in Abu Dhabi is an important milestone as it establishes the city as an “important destination on the international art market calendar.”

In 2024, Sotheby’s announced that it closed a deal worth $1 billion with Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund and investment company, ADQ, that saw them acquire a minority stake in the auction house. At the time, the auction house said that $800 million of the cash injection had been earmarked for paying down Sotheby’s $1.65 billion long-term debt, while the remainder of the money would support expansion plans, both in terms of real estate in the US and abroad, and the development of new markets and revenue streams. Now, Sotheby’s wants to show the fruits of its labor.

Mohammed Hafiz, cofounder of the Jeddah-based ATHR Gallery, told ARTnews that this is ultimately a cultural and a commercial decision. “The market has reached a scale where a local presence makes strategic and economic sense,” he said, noting that Art Dubai and Abu Dhabi Art (rebranded as Frieze Abu Dhabi) have been established for almost two decades now, and Christie’s is marking 20 years in the region with its first fine art auction on November 1. Hafiz said these developments in the Middle East are not new, but the result of decades-long investment and market building by patrons, galleries, collectors, artists and institutions, with the arrival of Art Basel and Frieze a natural evolution.

Philip Hoffman, chairman and founder of the Fine Art Group, told ARTnews that most of his big collectors will be going to Abu Dhabi in December for all the coinciding events. He noted that such a modest sale reflects buyers’ habits in the region, especially younger collectors in their 30s and 40s who are getting “super interested” but “want to take it easy and not rush. They don’t make quick decisions. I think auctions put a lot of pressure on them to make decisions and that’s not their natural habitat.”

At Sotheby’s, there has been a “real evolution in the collector landscape” in the Middle East, said Boueiz. She has noticed that clients have gone from appreciating art to engaging with it. In terms of the lots in “Breaking Ground,” Yasmeen Gailani, Sotheby’s specialist and head of sale for “Breaking Ground,” said the house wanted to anchor the sale with household names that resonate globally, alongside the household names in the Middle East.

“Many of these names will be new to our clients here, but that is part of what makes it all so exciting. We wanted to not only offer the works we know will immediately spark a conversation, but also provide the sort of setting where our clients here can discover artists that have never been offered in the Middle East before,” said Gailani.

Hafiz agreed that although collecting has always been deeply rooted in the culture of the region, it’s only in the last two decades that modern and contemporary art have had growing interest. As museums, foundations, and biennials have been established in the region, it has changed the relationship collectors have had with art, and it’s being passed down generations.

“We are also seeing collecting extend beyond a relatively small circle of established patrons to a younger and more diverse audience, with growing confidence in regional artists and an increasing interest in international practices,” said Hafiz.

editorial_title_zh: 里昂双年展迎来新馆长：Hélia Paukner 将自 2027 年起上任

article_text:
Hélia Paukner sarà la nuova direttrice artistica della Biennale d’arte contemporanea di Lione . La curatrice, attualmente responsabile del polo Arte contemporanea del Mucem di Marsiglia, assumerà ufficialmente l’incarico il primo febbraio 2027, succedendo a Isabelle Bertolotti , alla guida artistica della manifestazione dal 2018. La selezione è arrivata al termine di un processo di candidatura condotto dalla Ville de Lyon insieme al Ministero francese della Cultura, alla Métropole de Lyon e alla Biennale de Lyon.

La nomina alla Biennale di Lione avrà una doppia valenza: Hélia Paukner diventerà infatti anche direttrice del macLYON – Musée d’art contemporain de Lyon , confermando e rafforzando il rapporto strutturale tra il museo e la manifestazione, due istituzioni che da tempo condividono programmazione, spazi e strategie per l’arte contemporanea nella città francese.

La Biennale di Lione alla vigilia del nuovo corso

Fondata nel 1991 e attualmente presieduta da Laurent Bayle , la Biennale di Lione ha costruito negli anni una sua posizione preminente nel panorama dell’arte contemporanea internazionale, attraverso il contributo di curatori internazionali come Hans Ulrich Obrist, Hou Hanru, Gunnar B. Kvaran, Ralph Rugoff, Emma Lavigne, Jean de Loisy, Sam Bardaouil e Till Fellrath . L’organizzazione alterna annualmente l’appuntamento dedicato all’arte contemporanea con la Biennale de la Danse, oggi diretta da Tiago Guedes .

Il cambio alla direzione arriverà subito dopo la conclusione della 18ma edizione, attualmente in corso fino al 13 dicembre 2026, intitolata Passer d’un rêve à l’autre / To pass from one dream to another e curata da Catherine Nichols . Il progetto prende spunto dalle traboules di Lione, i caratteristici passaggi pedonali coperti che attraversano cortili privati di edifici, utilizzando la struttura economica, industriale e relazionale della città come punto di partenza per una riflessione sulle forme attraverso cui valore, lavoro, cura e immaginazione vengono prodotti e messi in circolazione. La mostra si sviluppa tra sedi differenti, dalle Grandes Locos al macLYON fino al Musée des Tissus.

Dal Mucem alla Biennale di Lione

Per Paukner si tratta anche di un ritorno a Lione, città nella quale si è formata e dove ha avviato le prime esperienze professionali. Nata nel 1983, dopo gli studi all’École normale supérieure de Lyon e successivamente all’Institut national du patrimoine di Parigi, ha mosso i primi passi curatoriali proprio al Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, dove ha lavorato come assistente di ricerca della direzione.

Dal 2019 è al Mucem – Musée des civilisations de l’Europe et de la Méditerranée di Marsiglia, dove ricopre il ruolo di conservatrice e responsabile del polo Arte contemporanea. Qui ha sviluppato progetti che intrecciano pratiche artistiche, ricerca antropologica e questioni sociali, occupandosi anche delle collezioni dedicate all’hip hop e ai graffiti. Ha anche dato impulso ad alcune delle acquisizioni più importanti, come una collezione delle ultime opere che Michel Journiac (1935-1995) realizzò sul tema dell’AIDS.

Tra i progetti seguiti figurano Affleurements , realizzato nell’ambito del programma europeo Excavating Contemporary Archaeology , la più grande retrospettiva in Francia dedicata a Ghada Amer tra il 2022 e il 2023, le mostre di Clément Cogitore e di Laure Prouvost e, più recentemente, la partecipazione al progetto espositivo dedicato a Don Quichotte .

Paukner ha inoltre fatto parte del gruppo curatoriale della mostra permanente Méditerranées , con la quale il Mucem rilegge la storia e le rappresentazioni del Mediterraneo attraverso collezioni, opere e materiali appartenenti a epoche differenti.

Tra radicamento locale e reti internazionali

Secondo quanto comunicato dalla Biennale, il nuovo corso dovrebbe svilupparsi attorno a tre assi principali: rafforzamento delle reti internazionali, maggiore connessione con il territorio lionese e sperimentazione di nuove forme di collaborazione artistica. Tra gli obiettivi dichiarati figurano anche l’ampliamento dei pubblici, la condivisione delle conoscenze e la costruzione di nuovi rapporti tra artisti, istituzioni e comunità.

La doppia responsabilità tra Biennale e macLYON dovrebbe inoltre permettere una maggiore continuità tra il lavoro museale e quello dell’esposizione periodica, superando almeno in parte la separazione tra programmazione istituzionale stabile e grande appuntamento internazionale.
